title: Python Api
description: HTTP, REST APIs, requests, nested JSON parsing, auth headers, pagination and API projects.

lessons.title: What is an API
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 1: What is an API

theory.contentHtml:
Open a weather app and you see "Hanoi 32°C". That number was not sitting inside your phone: the app just sent a request to the weather service's server and got the latest data back. Job boards work the same way - the listings live in their database, and besides the web page for human readers, many systems open a second door for programs: an API. Your program sends a request to an agreed address, and the server returns raw data in a format both sides settled on beforehand.

Request and response

Every exchange has two halves. The asking side - called the client, which can be a phone app, a browser, or your Python script - sends a request: what data it wants, at which address. The answering side - the server - processes it and sends back a response carrying the result. This whole course is about writing the client side well: composing correct requests and reading responses cleanly.

Endpoints: one address per kind of data

A server does not have a single door. An API splits its data across sub-addresses called endpoints - for example, the jobs API used in this course (you start calling it next chapter) has:

  • https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs - the list of job postings
  • https://api.xomdata.dev/me - the currently signed-in account

The https://api.xomdata.dev part is the shared base; each endpoint appends its own path. Ask a given endpoint, get that kind of data.

What the returned data looks like

A response meant for programs is structured text rather than a web page; the most common format is JSON:

{
  "jobs": [
    {"id": 1, "title": "Data Analyst", "city": "Hanoi"},
    {"id": 2, "title": "Data Engineer", "city": "Ho Chi Minh"}
  ]
}

Curly braces, key–value pairs, lists in square brackets - very close to the Python dicts and lists you already know. Close, but not the same thing yet: JSON is a text string, while a dict is a structure in Python's memory. The next lesson is about moving between the two.

lessons.title: JSON the common language of APIs
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 2: JSON the common language of APIs

theory.contentHtml:
The previous lesson stopped at the fact that API data arrives as a JSON text string. You cannot pull fields out of a string - text["title"] on a string is an immediate error. To work with it, you have to turn the string into dicts and lists, and the standard json library does exactly that.

From a JSON string to Python: json.loads

import json

text = '{"title": "Data Analyst", "city": "Hanoi", "remote": false, "salary": null}'
job = json.loads(text)
print(type(job))
print(job["title"])
print(job["salary"])
<class 'dict'>
Data Analyst
None

json.loads reads the string and builds the matching Python structure: an object {} becomes a dict, an array [] becomes a list, strings and numbers stay as they are, true/false become True/False, and null becomes None. Note the last line of the example: the salary field in the JSON is null - this posting does not state a salary - and in Python it is None, not the number 0 and not an empty string.

The return type follows the input. A JSON string that opens with [ gives you a list:

import json

cities = json.loads('["Hanoi", "Da Nang", "Ho Chi Minh"]')
print(cities[0])
print(len(cities))
Hanoi
3

The other direction: json.dumps

When you need to send data out (the chapter on POST will use this), json.dumps turns a dict/list into a JSON string:

import json

alert = {"city": "Hanoi", "active": True, "note": None}
print(json.dumps(alert))
{"city": "Hanoi", "active": true, "note": null}

This direction swaps the symbols too: True is written as true, None as null - the resulting string is JSON, no longer Python. The two functions are a pair: loads to read data you receive, dumps to compose data you send. In the practice lesson right after this, you get a JSON string exactly as an API would hand it over and turn it into a dict to extract information.

lessons.title: Quiz APIs and JSON
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 5: Quiz APIs and JSON

questions.prompt: What is an API for?

options.label: A
options.text: It is where two programs exchange data: the client sends a request, the server returns a result

options.label: B
options.text: It is a programming language designed specifically for building websites

options.label: C
options.text: It is a copy of the server's database downloaded onto your machine in advance

options.label: D
options.text: It is a tool for drawing interfaces that display data to end users

questions.explanation: An API is a channel for programs to talk to programs: the client composes a request to an agreed address, the server processes it and returns a response carrying the data. It is not a programming language - you still write Python and simply use the API as a place to get data. Nor does it copy the database onto your machine: the data stays on the server, and every question is a fresh exchange. And presenting things to human readers is the job of the web page or app - an API serves programs and returns raw data, it does not draw interfaces.

questions.prompt: JSON has the value null. After json.loads, what does it become in Python?

options.label: A
options.text: The number 0, because null means no meaningful value

options.label: B
options.text: The empty string "", because null is text with no content

options.label: C
options.text: None - the Python value meaning there is no data in that spot

options.label: D
options.text: False, because null in JSON is a boolean value

questions.explanation: JSON's null maps straight to Python's None - both say the same thing: there is no data here. Keeping that apart from the number 0 or an empty string matters in data work: a job posting with salary null means the salary is undisclosed, which is very different from a posting that pays 0. False is not it either: JSON has true/false of its own for booleans, while null is a separate value.

questions.prompt: What type does calling json.loads on a valid JSON string return?

options.label: A
options.text: Always a dict, because every JSON document is an object

options.label: B
options.text: It depends on the input: a string opening with { gives a dict, one opening with [ gives a list

options.label: C
options.text: Always a string, cleaned of the extra punctuation

options.label: D
options.text: Always a list whose elements are key–value pairs

questions.explanation: json.loads builds exactly the structure the string describes, so the result type follows the input: an object gives a dict, an array gives a list - and a string holding a lone number or JSON string gives exactly that type too. So neither "always a dict" nor "always a list" holds: many APIs wrap their data in an outer object, but a bare array is just as valid. A string result would defeat the point of the function entirely - it exists to escape string form and reach Python structures.

questions.prompt: Why use json.loads instead of slicing a JSON string yourself with split?

options.label: A
options.text: Because split runs much slower than json.loads on long strings

options.label: B
options.text: Because Python does not allow calling split on strings that contain curly braces

options.label: C
options.text: Because json.loads understands JSON syntax: reordered fields or values containing commas are all read correctly

options.label: D
options.text: Because split only works when the string fits on a single line

questions.explanation: Hand-slicing relies on surface appearance: it guesses that commas separate fields, and it guesses wrong the moment a title like "Data Engineer, Platform" carries a comma inside, or the server reorders the fields. json.loads parses by actual JSON syntax, so those cases all come out right. The reason is not speed, and Python forbids split on no string at all - split runs fine on multi-line strings and strings with braces, it just produces answers you cannot trust.

questions.prompt: What is an endpoint of an API?

options.label: A
options.text: A specific address on the server, with each endpoint in charge of one kind of data

options.label: B
options.text: The name of the Python function you must define to receive the data

options.label: C
options.text: The number the server returns to signal the exchange has finished

options.label: D
options.text: The data file saved onto your machine once the exchange is done

questions.explanation: An endpoint is a sub-address on the server - like /jobs for the list of postings or /me for the signed-in account - and asking a given endpoint gets you that kind of data. It belongs to the server side; it is not a Python function you write on the client. The number reporting how an exchange went is the status code, a different concept you will meet a lot next chapter. And API exchanges happen in your program's memory - no file is saved to your machine automatically.

lessons.title: Your first API call with requests
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 6: Your first API call with requests

theory.contentHtml:
The job listings you see on a recruitment site live in their database, and the web page is just one way to display them. Many systems open a second door: an API - send a request to an agreed address and receive JSON data back instead of a web page. The requests library does it in two lines:

import requests

r = requests.get("https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs")
print(r.status_code)
200

Network-calling blocks in the reading have no Run button - you will make this call yourself in the practice lesson right after this one.

Status code: how the server answered

requests.get returns a Response object, and the first number to look at is status_code. 200 means the request succeeded and the response body carries the data you asked for. 404 means the address does not exist - usually a mistyped path. A later chapter meets more codes; for now the habit is enough: check the status code before reading the data.

Reading the data with .json()

The data sits in the response body. For an API that returns JSON, r.json() parses that body into Python structures:

data = r.json()
print(data["jobs"][0]["title"])
Data Analyst

What r.json() gives back is ordinary Python dicts and lists, so every element-access skill you already have works as is:

data = {"jobs": [
    {"id": 1, "title": "Data Analyst", "city": "Hanoi"},
    {"id": 2, "title": "Data Engineer", "city": "Ho Chi Minh"},
]}
print(len(data["jobs"]))
print(data["jobs"][1]["city"])
2
Ho Chi Minh

One thing worth knowing early: if the response body is not JSON (say the server returned an HTML error page), r.json() raises an error rather than returning a string. To inspect the raw body yourself, read r.text. The error-handling lesson in a later chapter comes back to this point.

headings.text: Status code: how the server answered
Reading the data with .json()

lessons.title: Filtering data with query parameters
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 8: Filtering data with query parameters

theory.contentHtml:
Your users ask ever more specific questions: yesterday they searched for "jobs in Ho Chi Minh", today it is "senior jobs in Ho Chi Minh" - two conditions at once. The dict you pass to params then holds two key-value pairs, and requests folds both into the URL:

import requests

r = requests.get(
    "https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs",
    params={"city": "Ho Chi Minh", "level": "senior"},
)
print(r.url)
https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs?city=Ho+Chi+Minh&level=senior

r.url shows the final URL that requests actually sent. When an API returns something other than you expected, print it first - quite often the function received the right arguments but the assembled URL is not what you had in mind, and seeing the real URL is the fastest way to know what you actually asked.

Spaces become plus signs

Look closely at the URL above: Ho Chi Minh turned into Ho+Chi+Minh. In a query string, + is one encoding for a space; you will also meet %20. Requests may requote some characters while preparing a manually assembled URL, but it cannot infer whether a hand-concatenated & is data or a parameter separator. Using params gives the query string the right structure and consistently encodes spaces and reserved characters.

Inside a query string

The part after the question mark is called the query string: key=value pairs, joined together by &. The rule is simple enough to describe in a few lines of Python - run it to see how a dict turns into the tail of a URL:

params = {"city": "Ho Chi Minh", "level": "senior"}
parts = []
for key, value in params.items():
    parts.append(key + "=" + value.replace(" ", "+"))
print("https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs?" + "&".join(parts))
https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs?city=Ho+Chi+Minh&level=senior

The block above is only there to help you read URLs, not the way to do it for real: when calling an API, hand the dict to params - requests also handles other special characters that this hand-rolled version does not cover.

lessons.title: Quiz Calling APIs with requests
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 10: Quiz Calling APIs with requests

questions.prompt: What does requests.get("https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs") return?

options.label: A
options.text: A raw JSON string that you must parse yourself with json.loads

options.label: B
options.text: A Response object: status_code tells the outcome, .json() gets the data

options.label: C
options.text: An already-parsed dict of data, ready for element access right away

options.label: D
options.text: A temporary file holding the downloaded content, to be opened with open()

questions.explanation: requests.get wraps the whole exchange in one Response object: the status lives in status_code, and the body comes out through .json() or .text. The dict is therefore exactly one .json() call away rather than ready-made; the raw string is not what you hold directly either - it sits in .text - and there is no need to run json.loads yourself when .json() already does that. No file gets written to your machine - everything stays in the program's memory.

questions.prompt: You call an API and receive a status_code of 404. What does that mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The server hit an internal error; wait a moment and the retry will work

options.label: B
options.text: The request succeeded but the result list is empty

options.label: C
options.text: The address you asked for does not exist on the server

options.label: D
options.text: You have not authenticated, so the server refused to answer

questions.explanation: 404 is the server's answer that the path you asked for is not there - usually a mistyped endpoint, and calling again any number of times changes nothing. An internal error worth waiting-and-retrying carries code 500, while missing authentication is 401. As for a successful call with no results, the API still returns 200 with an empty list - status codes speak about the exchange, not about how much data came back.

questions.prompt: Why pass params={"city": "Brighton & Hove"} instead of concatenating that value into the URL yourself?

options.label: A
options.text: requests encodes a reserved character such as & as value data rather than a parameter separator

options.label: B
options.text: String concatenation makes the request noticeably slower to send

options.label: C
options.text: The API can only read parameters produced by requests; hand-concatenated ones are ignored

options.label: D
options.text: requests.get does not accept URLs that already contain a question mark

questions.explanation: params lets requests build and encode the query string correctly. Requests may requote a space in a hand-built URL, but that approach can still corrupt data containing a reserved character such as &: it may be interpreted as a parameter separator. If both approaches produce the same valid query string, the server cannot tell them apart - this is not about speed or an existing question mark.

questions.prompt: The response body is an HTML error page. What happens when you call r.json()?

options.label: A
options.text: It returns the HTML string untouched for you to handle yourself

options.label: B
options.text: It returns None to signal that there is no JSON data

options.label: C
options.text: It raises an error because the body cannot be parsed as JSON

options.label: D
options.text: It returns an empty dict {} and skips the unreadable body

questions.explanation: .json() parses the response body as JSON, and HTML is not JSON, so the parse fails with a raised error - deliberate behaviour, because quietly returning None or an empty dict would hide the problem until somewhere else in the program. To look at the raw body and understand what happened, read r.text - that is where the untouched HTML string lives.

chapters.title: FROM NESTED JSON TO A TABLE

lessons.title: Nested JSON dicts inside dicts
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 11: Nested JSON dicts inside dicts

theory.contentHtml:
In the previous module every job posting had just three fields: id, title, city. From this module on the API also returns company information, and the postings start to look like the real-world data you will meet: the company field is a dict sitting inside the posting dict.

job = {
    "id": 1,
    "title": "Data Analyst",
    "city": "Hanoi",
    "salary": 1200,
    "company": {"name": "VNG", "size": "large"},
}
print(job["company"])
print(job["company"]["name"])
{'name': 'VNG', 'size': 'large'}
VNG

Reading the path from the outside in

Each pair of square brackets goes one level deeper. job["company"] returns the whole inner dict {'name': 'VNG', 'size': 'large'}; for the company name, ask the inner level next: job["company"]["name"]. Read left to right, and at every step ask yourself "what did I just get back" - if it is a dict, the next step is another key.

Lists of dicts, dicts inside dicts

The response of GET /jobs mixes both kinds of nesting: {"jobs": [...]} - the value under the jobs key is a list, each element of that list is a posting dict, and inside each posting sits the company dict. Look at the opening character when you print something to know what you are holding: [ is a list - take elements by position or walk it with a loop; { is a dict - take values by key name.

data = {"jobs": [
    {"title": "Data Analyst", "company": {"name": "VNG"}},
    {"title": "Data Engineer", "company": {"name": "Tiki"}},
]}
for job in data["jobs"]:
    print(job["company"]["name"])
VNG
Tiki

This is exactly what r.json() will hand you in the next practice: a nested structure, and your job is to follow the right path to the value you need.

headings.text: Reading the path from the outside in
Lists of dicts, dicts inside dicts

lessons.title: Missing fields and null values
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 13: Missing fields and null values

theory.contentHtml:
Call this course's GET /jobs and you will see the "BI Analyst" posting has "salary": null - this company does not publish a salary. Real data is full of gaps like that, and code that does not plan for the gaps breaks exactly when it runs on real data.

null becomes None in Python

r.json() translates null into None. The salary field still exists in the dict - its value is just empty:

job = {"id": 3, "title": "BI Analyst", "salary": None}
print(job["salary"])
print(job["salary"] is None)
None
True

Adding None to a number or comparing it for size fails immediately, so before using a field that can be null, check is not None first.

Absent keys: [key] raises, .get does not

The second kind of gap is different: the key does not exist in the dict at all. Postings from this API have no bonus field, so asking with square brackets stops the program:

job["bonus"]   # KeyError: 'bonus'

.get asks the same question without raising - if the key is absent it returns None, or the default value you pass along:

job = {"id": 3, "title": "BI Analyst", "salary": None}
print(job.get("bonus"))
print(job.get("bonus", 0))
print(job.get("salary", 0))
None
0
None

The last line is worth a pause: salary is in the dict with the value None, so .get("salary", 0) returns None, not 0 - the default only kicks in when the key is absent altogether. Two kinds of gaps, two tools: a key that may be absent gets .get, a value that may be null gets an is not None check.

headings.text: null becomes None in Python
Absent keys: [key] raises, .get does not

GET https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs - without query params it returns all postings.

{

{'title': 'Data Analyst', 'company': 'VNG', 'city': 'Hanoi'}

lessons.title: Quiz Nested JSON
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 16: Quiz Nested JSON

questions.prompt: Given job = {"title": "Data Analyst", "company": {"name": "VNG", "size": "large"}}. Which expression gets "VNG"?

options.label: A
options.text: job["company"]["name"]

options.label: B
options.text: job["company.name"]

options.label: C
options.text: job["name"]

options.label: D
options.text: job["company", "name"]

questions.explanation: Each pair of square brackets goes one level deeper: job["company"] returns the inner dict, then ["name"] takes the name inside it. The string "company.name" is read by the dict as ONE literal key - Python dicts do not treat a dot as a path; "name" only exists at the inner level, so asking the outer level directly is a KeyError; and job["company", "name"] passes a whole tuple as a single key, which does not exist in the dict either.

questions.prompt: The dict job has no "bonus" key. How does job.get("bonus") differ from job["bonus"]?

options.label: A
options.text: .get returns None, while square brackets raise a KeyError

options.label: B
options.text: Both give the same result, .get is just the older spelling

options.label: C
options.text: .get adds the bonus key to the dict with the value None

options.label: D
options.text: Square brackets return an empty string, .get returns 0

questions.explanation: Square brackets insist the key must be there - if it is not, the program stops with a KeyError, while .get asks the same question gently: an absent key yields None, or the default value if you pass one along. So the two differ exactly in the absent-key case; it is not a matter of old versus new syntax. .get also only reads - it writes nothing into the dict - and neither way invents an empty string or a zero you never asked for.

questions.prompt: The API returns "salary": null. After r.json(), what is that value in Python?

options.label: A
options.text: None - to use this field you must check is not None first

options.label: B
options.text: The string "null" - check it by comparing == "null"

options.label: C
options.text: The number 0 - adding it to other salaries still works fine

options.label: D
options.text: The salary key is dropped from the dict - only .get can see it

questions.explanation: JSON's null is translated into Python's None - a genuinely empty value, neither a string nor a number, so adding or comparing it fails immediately; that is why you check is not None before using it. The easy mix-up: the salary key still sits in the dict with the value None - a present-but-empty field is different from an absent field, and .get only helps with the absent case; it cannot turn None into a usable value.

questions.prompt: Why do we usually flatten nested JSON before putting it into an analysis table?

options.label: A
options.text: Table cells hold simple values - a nested dict cannot go into a column

options.label: B
options.text: Nested JSON takes many times more memory, so it must be compressed

options.label: C
options.text: Python cannot read dicts nested more than two levels, so they must be split

options.label: D
options.text: The API requires clients to flatten the data before calling the next page

questions.explanation: An analysis table lives on cells with simple values - numbers, strings, dates - so it can filter, group, and compute by column; put a nested dict into a cell and those operations stop making sense. Flattening pulls the fields you need (like the company name inside company) out into their own columns. Memory is not the reason - both shapes hold the same data; Python reads dicts nested to any depth just fine; and the API stands entirely outside this: what it returns is its business, flattening is the analyst's.

lessons.title: Headers and auth tokens
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 17: Headers and auth tokens

theory.contentHtml:
Every endpoint you have called so far in this course is public - anyone who asks gets an answer. GET /me, the endpoint that returns your account details, is different: the server needs to know who you are first. Try calling it bare:

import requests

r = requests.get("https://api.xomdata.dev/me")
print(r.status_code)
401

401 is a refusal: the request has not been authenticated. To get through this door, you attach a token - a secret string the API issued to you personally - in the request headers. (Network-calling blocks in the reading have no Run button - you will send the token yourself in the practice right after.)

Headers: information that travels with the request

Besides the URL, every HTTP request carries a set of headers - name–value pairs describing the request. requests accepts them through the headers= parameter as a plain dict:

headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer xom-live-8f3a"}
r = requests.get("https://api.xomdata.dev/me", headers=headers)
print(r.status_code)
print(r.json()["user"]["plan"])
200
premium

Bearer tokens in the Authorization header

The Authorization header has a prescribed shape: the scheme name, one space, then the credentials. For tokens the scheme is Bearer:

token = "xom-live-8f3a"
headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + token}
print(headers["Authorization"])
Bearer xom-live-8f3a

Leave out the word Bearer, drop the space, or mistype the token - the server answers 401 all the same, so when you get refused, this header's value is the first place to look. And as always: check status_code before reading data, because the body of a 401 is an error message, not what you were waiting for.

Keep tokens out of source code

The course uses a fake token so examples stay reproducible. For a real token, do not paste it into a Python file or commit it to Git. Read it from an environment variable:

import os
import requests

token = os.environ["API_TOKEN"]
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}
r = requests.get("https://api.example.com/me", headers=headers, timeout=10)

If you use a local .env file, keep it in .gitignore; in production, use the platform's environment variables or secret manager.

Never put the token in the URL

A token is the key to an account. URLs are commonly recorded in server and proxy logs and browser history, so a token in the query string leaves an especially broad trail. The Authorization header is the standard place, but that does not mean headers can never be logged: a proxy, middleware layer or debug logger can still record it when configured badly. Redact sensitive headers and never dump a complete request into logs.

headings.text: Headers: information that travels with the request
Bearer tokens in the Authorization header
Keep tokens out of source code
Never put the token in the URL

lessons.title: Sending data with POST
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 19: Sending data with POST

theory.contentHtml:
So far every call you have made is a GET: ask and receive. But when a student wants to be notified the moment a new Data Analyst job appears in Hanoi, the data flows the other way - you send the registration details up so the server can create a new record. Creating things is what the POST method is for:

import requests

alert = {"city": "Hanoi", "level": "junior"}
r = requests.post("https://api.xomdata.dev/alerts", json=alert)
print(r.status_code)
201

The json= parameter

json= takes a dict, turns it into a JSON string placed in the request body, and sets the Content-Type: application/json header for you so the server knows how to read that body. The conversion itself is the json.dumps you met in module 1:

import json

alert = {"city": "Hanoi", "level": "junior"}
body = json.dumps(alert)
print(body)
print(type(body).__name__)
{"city": "Hanoi", "level": "junior"}
str

You could call json.dumps yourself and send the string through data=, but then requests does not set Content-Type for you and many APIs will refuse to read the body. json= is the shorter path and the harder one to get wrong.

201: created

With GET, success is 200. POST creating something new has its own code: 201 says the request led to the creation of a new resource on the server. APIs usually return the freshly created record in the response body, including the id they just assigned:

print(r.json())
{'id': 101, 'city': 'Hanoi', 'level': 'junior', 'active': True}

That id is what your program carries away for later use - updating or deleting the alert afterwards happens through that number. And if the body you sent is missing a required field, the API answers 400: the mistake is on the sender's side, so fix the body and send again - repeating the identical call will not help.

headings.text: The json= parameter
201: created

lessons.title: Quiz Authentication and POST
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 21: Quiz Authentication and POST

questions.prompt: To call an API that authenticates with a token, what shape must the Authorization header value take?

options.label: A
options.text: "xom-live-8f3a" - just the token string, nothing else

options.label: B
options.text: "Bearer xom-live-8f3a" - scheme name, a space, then the token

options.label: C
options.text: "Bearer=xom-live-8f3a" - joined with an equals sign, query-string style

options.label: D
options.text: "xom-live-8f3a Bearer" - token first, scheme name after

questions.explanation: The standard shape of this header is the scheme name, one space, then the credentials - for tokens the scheme is Bearer, so the full value is "Bearer xom-live-8f3a". A bare token has no scheme, so the server cannot tell which kind of authentication the string is meant to be; the equals sign is query-string syntax, not header syntax; and putting the token first means the leading part is no longer a valid scheme. All three variants earn the same 401 as sending nothing at all.

questions.prompt: You call the right endpoint address but your token has expired. Which code does the server return?

options.label: A
options.text: 404, because the server cannot find your data

options.label: B
options.text: 400, because the request body you sent is invalid

options.label: C
options.text: 401, because the request was not successfully authenticated

options.label: D
options.text: 500, because the server hit an error while checking the token

questions.explanation: The endpoint exists and the server understands the request - the only thing wrong is authentication, and the code reserved for that is 401. 404 is about an address that does not exist, meaning you typed the wrong path, not the wrong token. 400 is about an invalid request body, and this GET call sends no body at all. 500 means the failure is on the server's side, whereas here the server is working exactly as designed: it is refusing you on purpose.

questions.prompt: What does the json= parameter of requests.post do?

options.label: A
options.text: Turns the dict into a JSON body and sets the matching Content-Type header

options.label: B
options.text: Parses the response body into a dict so you can skip calling r.json()

options.label: C
options.text: Sends the dict as form data, exactly like the data= parameter does

options.label: D
options.text: Only sets the Content-Type header; the data still has to be packed by hand

questions.explanation: json= handles the entire sending side: it turns the dict into a JSON string placed in the request body and sets Content-Type: application/json as well. It has nothing to do with the receiving side - parsing the response is still r.json()'s job. data= is the one that sends form data, and that difference is exactly why json= exists. The only-sets-the-header option describes half of the work: packing the data is the main part this parameter takes off your hands.

questions.prompt: What does a 201 code after a POST call tell you?

options.label: A
options.text: The request was received but the server has not finished processing it

options.label: B
options.text: The request succeeded but the response carries no body

options.label: C
options.text: A new resource was created as a result of your request

options.label: D
options.text: The data you sent duplicates a record that already exists

questions.explanation: 201 Created means the request led to the creation of a new resource - the expected outcome of a POST that makes a record, and servers usually include the freshly created record in the response body. A 201 means the creation is already done, so received-but-not-processed is not what it says. The body of a 201 carries data as usual - the practice reads the id from exactly that body. And sending a duplicate of an existing record is an error case, which must carry a 4xx code, never a success code.

questions.prompt: Why should a token never go into the query string of a URL?

options.label: A
options.text: URLs are written into server logs and browser history, and the token stays there

options.label: B
options.text: Query strings have a length limit, so a long token would get cut off

options.label: C
options.text: Servers have no way to read values placed in the query string

options.label: D
options.text: A token in the URL makes the request noticeably slower to encrypt

questions.explanation: URLs are commonly recorded in server and proxy logs and browser history, so a query-string token leaves a broader trail than necessary. The Authorization header is the standard location, but it must still be redacted because misconfigured middleware or debug logging can record headers too. Servers can read query strings perfectly well; this is about reducing exposure, not about headers being immune to logs.

lessons.title: Status codes reading the server's answer
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 22: Status codes reading the server's answer

theory.contentHtml:
You write a function that fetches one job's details, run it, and r.json() gives back something unexpected. Printing r.status_code reveals what happened: the server answered 404 because the URL is missing one letter, and the response body is an error message with no job in it. The status code tells you whether the request succeeded, and if not, how it failed - so read it before touching the data.

import requests

r = requests.get("https://api.xomdata.dev/job/1")  # typo: should be /jobs/1
print(r.status_code)
404

Network-calling blocks in the reading have no Run button - you will handle these codes yourself in the practice right after.

Three families of codes

Status codes group by their first digit. The 2xx family means success: 200 for a GET with data, 201 when something was created. The 4xx family signals a client-side or server-policy condition that needs attention: codes such as 400, 401, 403, and 404 normally require a corrected request or permission. That does not make every 4xx permanent: 429 Too Many Requests may be retried later, honoring Retry-After when present. The 5xx family means the server is in trouble: 500 internal error, 503 overloaded - your request may be perfectly fine, and retrying a moment later can work.

for code in [200, 201, 404, 401, 500, 503]:
    print(code, "->", str(code)[0] + "xx")
200 -> 2xx
201 -> 2xx
404 -> 4xx
401 -> 4xx
500 -> 5xx
503 -> 5xx

Check before reading the data

Many APIs return a JSON body even on errors (for example {"error": "not found"}), so r.json() runs fine while what's inside is an error message - the code further down is what breaks. So branch on the code first, read the data second:

r = requests.get("https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs/1")
if r.status_code == 200:
    print(r.json()["job"]["title"])
else:
    print("request failed:", r.status_code)

raise_for_status: turning error codes into exceptions

Checking by hand everywhere is easy to forget. r.raise_for_status() does it in one move: on a 4xx/5xx code it raises requests.exceptions.HTTPError, and on a success code it does nothing at all. Put it right after the call and HTTP errors blow up on the spot instead of sneaking down to wherever the data is used:

r = requests.get("https://api.xomdata.dev/job/1")
r.raise_for_status()
# requests.exceptions.HTTPError: 404 Client Error: ...
data = r.json()  # only runs when the status is good

The next practice uses the manual check - it lets you decide what to do with each code, instead of stopping the whole program.

Check before reading the data
raise_for_status: turning error codes into exceptions

lessons.title: Slow networks timeouts and retries
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 24: Slow networks timeouts and retries

theory.contentHtml:
Your data-collection script runs at 2 AM. At 8 you check on it: no error, no result, the program is still sitting on one requests.get call from six hours ago. The requests documentation states the reason plainly: without a timeout, a request never expires on its own - however long the server stays silent, your program waits.

Setting a deadline with timeout

r = requests.get("https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs", timeout=5)

If the connection cannot be established in time, or the socket receives no bytes for 5 seconds, the call raises requests.exceptions.Timeout instead of waiting on - and your program gets to decide the next step: report, skip, or retry. The official docs advise that nearly all production code should set this parameter. This is not a five-second deadline for the whole download: as long as data keeps arriving, the total duration can be longer.

Catching Timeout and retrying

Slow networks are usually only slow for a moment; calling again right after often works. Combining try/except with a loop gives you a retry mechanism:

for attempt in range(3):
    try:
        r = requests.get("https://api.xomdata.dev/jobs", timeout=5)
        break
    except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
        print("attempt", attempt + 1, "timed out")

Timeout is just one member of the requests error family: a dropped connection raises ConnectionError, raise_for_status() raises HTTPError, and they all inherit from requests.exceptions.RequestException. Catching the parent is useful for reporting failures in one place, but it does not mean every failure deserves a retry: 400, 401, 403 and 404 normally require a corrected request or permission.

Back off, and retry only safe work

The range(3) above is deliberate. If the server is truly down, a hundred extra calls will not save it, while every retry piles more work onto exactly the place that is already overloaded. Production code needs three guardrails:

  • Back off between attempts, commonly 1 second, 2 seconds, 4 seconds; add random jitter when many workers may retry together.
  • Retry only transient failures: timeouts, broken connections, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504. Honor Retry-After when the response provides it.
  • Automatic retries are safest for idempotent methods such as GET. Retrying a POST can create the same record twice unless the API supports an idempotency key.

After the final attempt, raise the last error or return an intentional failure state; do not leave r undefined and fail later on an unrelated line. The practice sandbox does not really sleep, so tests stay fast; it checks the attempt limit and failure result. The rhythm of one retry round looks like this:

attempts = ["timeout", "timeout", "ok"]
result = None
for i, outcome in enumerate(attempts, start=1):
    print("attempt", i, "->", outcome)
    if outcome == "ok":
        result = outcome
        break
print(result)
attempt 1 -> timeout
attempt 2 -> timeout
attempt 3 -> ok
ok

lessons.title: Data comes back one page at a time
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 26: Data comes back one page at a time

theory.contentHtml:
The course's jobs API holds 6 postings, so returning them all in one response is no burden. Real APIs are different: a large job board keeps hundreds of thousands of postings, and returning everything at once is slow and memory-hungry on both ends. So most list APIs cut the data into pages, one page per request.

What a paginated response looks like

Each page carries its own data plus the information needed to move on:

{
  "jobs": [
    {"id": 1, "title": "Data Analyst", "city": "Hanoi"},
    {"id": 2, "title": "Data Engineer", "city": "Ho Chi Minh"}
  ],
  "page": 1,
  "has_next": true
}

page says which page you are on, and has_next answers the most important question: is there another page after this one. To get the next page, call the same endpoint again with the page query param increased by 1.

The page-collecting loop

The structure is the same for every API of this kind: ask for page 1, collect the results, and as long as has_next is true, bump the page and ask again. Try that rhythm on data laid out as a dict:

pages = {
    1: {"jobs": ["Data Analyst", "Data Engineer"], "has_next": True},
    2: {"jobs": ["BI Analyst", "Analytics Engineer"], "has_next": True},
    3: {"jobs": ["Data Scientist", "ML Engineer"], "has_next": False},
}
titles = []
page = 1
while True:
    data = pages[page]
    titles.extend(data["jobs"])
    if not data["has_next"]:
        break
    page += 1
print(titles)
['Data Analyst', 'Data Engineer', 'BI Analyst', 'Analytics Engineer', 'Data Scientist', 'ML Engineer']

The stop condition is the most important part

A while True loop is only safe when you are certain there is a way out, and here the way out is has_next turning false on the last page - the API commits to that in its documentation. Do not replace it with a guess like "3 pages should be all of it": the page count changes with the data, right today and wrong next week. Ask past the last page and this API answers 404 - the very code you met at the start of this module. Next up in practice: collect every posting across all pages without knowing how many pages there are.

The page-collecting loop
The stop condition is the most important part

lessons.title: Quiz Errors, timeouts, and pagination
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 28: Quiz Errors, timeouts, and pagination

questions.prompt: Both mean a failed request - so how do codes 500 and 404 differ?

options.label: A
options.text: 500 is a server-side problem where waiting and retrying may succeed; 404 means the address does not exist and retrying changes nothing

options.label: B
options.text: 404 is a temporary server problem and 500 means a wrong path - both are worth retrying a few times

options.label: C
options.text: The two codes are equivalent: a failed request always means fixing the caller's code and running it again

options.label: D
options.text: 500 means the result set is empty, while 404 means the server refused because authentication was missing

questions.explanation: For the two codes in the question, 500 is a server failure that may be temporary, while a 404 for a missing path will not change if the same request is repeated. One may be worth retrying; the other calls for checking the URL. Do not generalize that to every 4xx: a 429 may be retried according to Retry-After. An empty result can still be 200 with a JSON body such as {"jobs": []}; missing authentication is 401.

questions.prompt: What does the timeout=5 parameter in requests.get(url, timeout=5) do?

options.label: A
options.text: Limits connection time and socket inactivity; it is not a deadline for the entire download

options.label: B
options.text: Demands that the server finish processing the request within 5 seconds, cancelling it server-side otherwise

options.label: C
options.text: Automatically repeats the request every 5 seconds until the server answers successfully

options.label: D
options.text: Spaces consecutive calls 5 seconds apart so the load on the server stays low

questions.explanation: timeout is a caller-side limit for connecting and for how long the socket may receive no bytes; requests.exceptions.Timeout lets the program react when that limit is crossed. It is not a cap on the whole download, and the server never sees the number, so it neither forces faster processing nor cancels server-side work. requests also does not retry or pace calls by itself - you write that loop explicitly.

questions.prompt: Why must a retry loop have a maximum number of attempts?

options.label: A
options.text: If the server is truly down, extra calls cannot save it - the program hangs forever while piling more load onto an overloaded system

options.label: B
options.text: requests enforces a rule that a program may retry the same endpoint at most three times

options.label: C
options.text: Each retry makes the server respond more slowly than the previous attempt, so retrying always loses

options.label: D
options.text: Retrying too many times makes the server permanently switch from code 500 to code 404

questions.explanation: Retrying only rescues transient hiccups. When the server is truly down, every extra call fails the same way, while your program sits stuck in the loop and the endless stream of requests piles more work onto exactly the weakest spot. Capping the attempts is how you acknowledge that: once they run out, stop and hand the failure to the caller to decide. The specific number is your choice for your problem - requests imposes no ceiling; retrying does not slow down individual responses, and no amount of calling changes which error code the server returns.

questions.prompt: What is the has_next field in a paginated response for?

options.label: A
options.text: It is the stop condition for the page-collecting loop: false means you are holding the last page

options.label: B
options.text: It says whether the current page holds more postings or fewer postings than the page before it

options.label: C
options.text: It signals upcoming server maintenance, so later pages may be temporarily unavailable

options.label: D
options.text: It counts exactly how many pages remain that the program has not downloaded yet

questions.explanation: has_next is the loop's control signal: true means there is more data after this page, so bump page and call again; false means you are holding the last page, and once it is collected you stop. It only answers yes-or-no - it does not count remaining pages, does not compare posting counts between pages, and says nothing about server maintenance. If an API wants to provide that kind of information, it lives in other fields of the response.

questions.prompt: The page-collecting loop is written as while True with no exit condition at all. What happens?

options.label: A
options.text: When the real data runs out, the loop keeps asking for pages that do not exist - the program hangs or dies with an error

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing bad: requests notices the server has run out of data and exits the loop for you

options.label: C
options.text: Python detects the infinite loop as soon as it runs and stops the program with a warning

options.label: D
options.text: The server sees the client asking repeatedly and merges all remaining pages into one response

questions.explanation: A loop only stops at an exit you wrote yourself. requests hands back one response at a time and does not steer your loop, Python has no infinite-loop detector, and the server cannot force a client to stop asking or merge pages on its own. When the real data runs out, the program keeps requesting page 4, page 5... - with the course API that is a string of 404s whose bodies no longer carry a jobs key, so depending on how the code is written the loop either dies with an error or hangs forever. The right way out is a stop condition based on the has_next of the page you just received.

chapters.title: PROJECT: FROM API TO ANALYSIS TABLE

lessons.title: Assembling the pipeline API to analysis table
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 29: Assembling the pipeline API to analysis table

theory.contentHtml:
Your manager asks a question that sounds simple: "how many job postings do we have in each city?". The data sits behind an API that returns one page at a time, and each posting nests the company details inside it. This chapter's project has no new material except the final piece - the real work is connecting what you already know into one complete run:

  1. Call the API page by page (chapter 5): loop page=1, 2, ... until has_next says you are done.
  2. Collect every page's results into a single list (chapter 2: params=, .json()).
  3. Flatten each posting: pull company["name"] up to a top-level field (chapter 3).
  4. Pour it into a table to count, group, and sort - the last piece, taught right below.

From a list of dicts to a DataFrame

pandas accepts a list of flat dicts directly: each dict becomes a row, each key becomes a column.

import pandas as pd

jobs = [
    {"title": "Data Analyst", "company": "VNG", "city": "Hanoi", "salary": 1200},
    {"title": "Data Engineer", "company": "Tiki", "city": "Ho Chi Minh", "salary": 2500},
    {"title": "BI Analyst", "company": "MoMo", "city": "Hanoi", "salary": None},
]
df = pd.DataFrame(jobs)
print(df)
print(df["city"].value_counts())
           title company         city  salary
0   Data Analyst     VNG        Hanoi  1200.0
1  Data Engineer    Tiki  Ho Chi Minh  2500.0
2     BI Analyst    MoMo        Hanoi     NaN
city
Hanoi          2
Ho Chi Minh    1
Name: count, dtype: int64

value_counts() counts rows for each distinct value in a column - your manager's question answered in one line. Look at the salary column too: the MoMo posting does not disclose a salary (None), so pandas records that cell as NaN and switches the whole column to floats - which is why 1200 shows up as 1200.0. NaN does not break calculations: df["salary"].mean() skips missing cells on its own.

Why flatten first

If you pour the nested JSON straight in, the company column ends up holding the entire dict {"name": ..., "size": ...}. The table raises no error, but a cell holding a whole block cannot be grouped or counted by company name. An analysis table needs every cell to be a single value - that is what the flattening step is for.

The next two practice lessons build exactly this pipeline on the course's jobs API: the first collects and flattens, the second pours the data into a table and answers your manager's question.

Write a function collect_jobs():

lessons.title: Calling real APIs beyond the course
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 32: Calling real APIs beyond the course

theory.contentHtml:
The course's jobs API is a training ground. Out in the world, the same skill set works immediately with thousands of public APIs - this lesson covers the three things you will meet on your very first call.

Documentation, API keys and rate limits

Every API has a documentation page listing endpoints, parameters, and sample responses - the same role as the "API documentation" section in the practice lessons, just much longer. Reading the docs before writing any code is the biggest time-saver this line of work has.

Many APIs require you to register an account to get an API key - an identifying string you send with every request, usually through a header like the Bearer token from chapter 4. The key comes with a rate limit: a cap on how many calls you can make within a time window. Call too fast and you get status 429 - when it appears, slow down instead of hammering the API in a loop.

Two good APIs to start with because they need no key:

  • Open-Meteo (api.open-meteo.com) - weather forecasts, all it needs is coordinates.
  • GitHub API (api.github.com) - public information about repos and users.
import requests

r = requests.get("https://api.github.com/repos/pandas-dev/pandas")
print(r.json()["stargazers_count"])

Run on your own machine (with Python and requests installed), the snippet above prints the current star count of the pandas repo.

Why the course sandbox cannot call outside APIs

The course editor runs Python right inside your browser, and browsers have a rule of their own: a page on one domain may only read data from another domain if that other server explicitly allows it (the CORS mechanism). Most APIs do not grant that permission - they serve programs running directly on a machine, not unknown web pages. That is why the practice lessons use a simulated server, while real APIs are for the Python installed on your own machine: no browser restrictions there, and the code is identical to what you have written throughout the course.

Ungraded homework: fetch the current temperature of your city from Open-Meteo, or count a GitHub user's public repos. The framework never changes: read the docs, try one endpoint, check the status code, then extract the data.

lessons.title: Quiz Capstone project
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 33: Quiz Capstone project

questions.prompt: In what order does this chapter's project pipeline run?

options.label: A
options.text: Call the API page by page → collect into one list → flatten each posting → pour into a DataFrame

options.label: B
options.text: Pour the raw JSON into a DataFrame first → flatten with pandas → then fetch the remaining pages

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the server to flatten in advance → the API returns a finished table → just print it

options.label: D
options.text: Turn each page into its own DataFrame → analyze each table → add the results together

questions.explanation: The data moves in a straight line: request each page in turn, collect everything into one list, flatten each posting into a one-level dict, and only then pour the whole list into a DataFrame at once. The server does not flatten for you - the nested structure is what the API returns, and handling it is your side's job. Pour raw JSON into a table first and the company column holds whole dicts, at which point pandas has nothing useful left to "flatten". And one DataFrame per page means counting by city requires adding results across tables by hand - exactly the work that collecting into one place up front saves you.

questions.prompt: Why flatten (pull the nested company name up to the top level) before building the table?

options.label: A
options.text: Because a DataFrame raises an error as soon as it meets any nested dict in the data

options.label: B
options.text: So every cell in the table is a single value, which makes grouping and counting by company name possible

options.label: C
options.text: Because nested data makes the table take many times more memory than the flat form

options.label: D
options.text: So the table has fewer columns, which makes printing to the screen faster

questions.explanation: The reason lies in what you plan to do with the table: grouping, counting, and sorting all operate on single values in cells. A DataFrame raises no error on a nested dict - it quietly stuffs the whole dict into one cell, and that quietness is the real trouble: the table looks fine once built, yet counting by company name no longer works. Memory and print speed are non-issues at this data size, and flattening actually adds columns rather than removing them.

questions.prompt: A salary field carrying None goes into a numeric DataFrame column. How does that cell show up?

options.label: A
options.text: NaN - pandas treats it as a missing cell, and the whole column switches to floats

options.label: B
options.text: The string "None" sitting in between the numbers in the column

options.label: C
options.text: The number 0, because pandas replaces every missing value with 0 when building the table

options.label: D
options.text: It does not show up - the row holding the missing value is dropped as the table is built

questions.explanation: In a numeric column, None becomes NaN - pandas' marker for a missing cell - and the column switches to floats, which is why 1200 shows as 1200.0. This behavior is worth having: calculations like mean() skip NaN on their own, whereas substituting 0 would silently drag the average salary down. The data row does not disappear either - a posting with no disclosed salary is still counted when you count postings per city; only its salary cell is empty.

questions.prompt: What decides when the page-collecting loop stops?

options.label: A
options.text: The has_next field in the response - the server saying false means the pages are done

options.label: B
options.text: A page count computed in advance from the dataset size you knew while writing the code

options.label: C
options.text: The moment a page comes back with fewer postings than the page right before it

options.label: D
options.text: A built-in safety cap on iterations that Python applies to every while loop

questions.explanation: The stop condition comes from the server itself: has_next is the data holder's statement about whether more pages exist, so it stays correct for any dataset size. Precompute the page count and the hard-coded number is wrong the moment a few postings are added. Comparing sizes of consecutive pages falls short too: when the total divides evenly by the page size, the last page is still full and that comparison never fires. And Python does not stop any while loop on its own - a loop without an exit condition runs forever, which is why chapter 5 insists on a clear way out.
